Dependent rubor is a reddish or dusky colour that appears when an ischaemic limb is lowered.
Mottling in an acutely painful, cold limb may indicate severe perfusion impairment.

blocks.text: Measure blood pressure using an appropriately sized cuff.

A significant inter-arm difference may suggest arterial disease, although technique and other causes must be considered.

The ankle–brachial pressure index compares ankle systolic pressure with brachial systolic pressure. It is useful in assessing lower-limb peripheral arterial disease.
\[ \text{ABI}= \frac{\text{Higher ankle systolic pressure in the tested leg}} {\text{Higher brachial systolic pressure}} \]
For the ankle measurement, the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries are usually assessed using a Doppler device.

An ABI above 1.40 can occur with arterial calcification, particularly in people with diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Toe pressure or toe–brachial index testing may be more useful in these circumstances.

Exam point: A normal resting ABI does not exclude all peripheral arterial disease. Exercise ABI, toe pressures or other vascular investigations may be needed when symptoms persist or results are inconclusive.

blocks.text: In acute limb ischaemia, sensory loss and motor weakness indicate a threatened limb and require immediate vascular assessment.
The classic features of acute limb ischaemia are the six Ps:
Pain
Sudden, often severe limb pain.
Pallor
Pale skin due to reduced arterial blood flow.
Poikilothermia
The affected limb becomes unusually cold.
Pulselessness
Peripheral pulses may be absent or diminished.
Paraesthesia
Tingling, altered sensation or numbness.
Paralysis
Weakness or inability to move the limb, a late and particularly concerning sign.
Not every patient presents with all six features. Do not wait for all six to appear before escalating a suspected acute arterial occlusion.
This is a high-yield examination topic, especially when assessing lower-limb ulcers.

May reduce venous oedema and discomfort

blocks.text: These are typical patterns, not absolute rules. Mixed arterial and venous disease is common, and a venous-appearing ulcer can still have an arterial component.

items.text: Intermittent claudication: Reproducible exertional limb pain that resolves with rest.
Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: Peripheral arterial disease associated with ischaemic rest pain, non-healing wounds or gangrene, requiring urgent vascular assessment.
Acute limb ischaemia: Sudden reduction in arterial perfusion, requiring emergency assessment.
Chronic venous insufficiency: Venous hypertension producing oedema, pigmentation, eczema and venous ulceration.
Lymphoedema: Persistent tissue swelling from impaired lymphatic drainage; it may become non-pitting as fibrosis develops.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. How to present normal peripheral vascular findings

blocks.text: Normal OSCE presentation

“Both upper and lower limbs are symmetrical, with normal skin colour and no ulcers, gangrene, significant oedema or trophic skin changes. The limbs are warm, and capillary refill is within the expected range. The radial, brachial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable and symmetrical. There are no clinically significant signs of peripheral arterial insufficiency or chronic venous disease.”
Copy normal presentation
Only state that all pulses are normal if you examined them. If the examination is restricted to the lower limbs, present those findings rather than claiming a normal upper-limb vascular examination.
A. Peripheral arterial disease

“The affected lower limb is cooler than the opposite side, with [pallor/trophic skin changes/ulceration]. The femoral pulse is [grade], the popliteal pulse is [grade], and the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are [grades]. These findings suggest impaired arterial perfusion. I would assess the limb's sensory and motor function and obtain Doppler assessment and appropriate vascular investigations.”
Copy presentation
B. Acute limb ischaemia

“The patient has a suddenly painful, cold and pale [right/left] limb, with diminished or absent distal pulses and [sensory/motor abnormalities, if present]. I am concerned about acute limb ischaemia and would arrange immediate vascular assessment.”

C. Chronic venous insufficiency

“There is [right/left/bilateral] lower-limb oedema, with brown pigmentation and [eczema/lipodermatosclerosis/ulceration] around the gaiter region. The peripheral pulses are [findings]. These features are consistent with chronic venous insufficiency, and I would assess for coexisting arterial disease.”

D. Suspected DVT

“There is unilateral [right/left] lower-limb swelling with [tenderness/warmth/erythema]. These findings raise suspicion of deep vein thrombosis but are not diagnostic. I would assess clinical probability and arrange the appropriate investigations, including compression ultrasonography when indicated.”

1. What are the major lower-limb pulses?
Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis.
2. What is intermittent claudication?
Exertional limb pain caused by inadequate blood supply during activity, which improves with rest.
3. What is the difference between arterial and venous ulcers?

Arterial ulcers often affect the toes or foot and may be painful with punched-out edges. Venous ulcers commonly affect the gaiter region and are associated with oedema, pigmentation and irregular edges.
4. What is the ABI?
The ratio of ankle systolic blood pressure to brachial systolic blood pressure, used to assess lower-limb arterial perfusion.
5. Why might the ABI be falsely elevated?
Non-compressible calcified arteries, particularly in people with diabetes or chronic kidney disease, may produce abnormally high ankle pressures.
6. What are the six Ps of acute limb ischaemia?
Pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paraesthesia and paralysis.
7. What is the difference between DVT and chronic venous insufficiency?

DVT is acute thrombosis of a deep vein and can cause unilateral swelling and pain. Chronic venous insufficiency results from sustained venous hypertension, often causing oedema, pigmentation, eczema and ulceration. The conditions are distinct but can be related.
8. Does a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse exclude peripheral arterial disease?
No. Peripheral arterial disease can exist despite palpable pulses, particularly when disease is mild or affects other arterial segments.
Remember the sequence:
Inspect → Temperature → Capillary refill → Pulses → Bruits when indicated → Venous assessment → Neurological assessment when indicated.
Always compare both limbs. The combination of symptoms, skin findings, pulse patterns and objective vascular measurements is more informative than any single sign.
